title: The Year I Was Born

paragraphs: “Have you become such a great man that you can now write your life story?” It was not someone else who asked me that question. My own heart asked it of me. But it had kept the answer in its own hands as well.
Does life—and history—belong only to the great? Do the small not own them too?

Every human being has a life story. He may never think of writing it down. He may have no time to write it. Or he may lack the skill to gather its scattered threads and shape them into a written account.

And yet two prisoners talk between themselves about the stories of their lives—we can hear them. Two elderly rickshaw pullers, resting in the shade of a tree and leaning comfortably against their vehicles, exchange the memorable episodes of their lives. Listen closely to two mendicants lying awake on the raised platform of a choultry, and there too what you hear is their life history.

A patient on his deathbed, knowing that his end has come, watches the story of his life circle soundlessly before his mind's eye. Unable to write it, unable even to speak it, he lets it run like a film within his own heart. The unbidden smile at the threshold of death, the deep sigh, the tear—each of these is a different chapter in his history.

An individual's history may contain no event that brought about a great social transformation. A political revolution may have found no place in his life. But in the changes and revolutions taking place in his country, he may have taken some part without even knowing it.

He is a part of society. People like him, taken together, are society—the country itself. Who can deny that truth? So, in one way or another, he has a share in the changes of his land, even if he never considered that share important enough to enter in the record of his own life.

In a storm that devastates an entire village, a branch torn from a tree is hurled through the air and crashes into the front of a house, bringing it down. What did the deed—the storm, or the branch? Whatever the answer, an event has entered the history of that branch.

Only after thinking through all this did I find the courage to render justice to my heart. The verdict itself came in the form of a question: “Does life—and history—belong only to the great? Do the small not own them too?”
After that verdict, my pen began its work without pause or obstruction.
My birthday was celebrated on the third of June. Thinking about birthdays, I could not help remembering what the thinker Rousseau had said: “My first misfortune was that I was born a human being!”
There is something curious about that great thinker—who taught all humanity how to safeguard the rights that come with birth—cursing and lamenting his own birth.

Perhaps the disorder of the home into which he was born, of his country, and of its political and social circumstances disturbed him deeply. Perhaps, remembering all that many years later, he grieved within himself: “Why was I born at all?”
My birth did not take place amid such circumstances.

My family was not steeped in wealth when I was born. But neither were my parents submerged up to the neck in the dark pit of poverty. My motherland was indeed bound in the fetters of slavery; yet it was not, like the France into which Rousseau was born, reeling without direction and racing towards destruction at a demonic speed.

Voltaire rejected Rousseau's notion that, just as a human being enters the world crying, he must spend the whole of life sobbing and wasting away without purpose. Like Voltaire, I too differ from Rousseau in my view of birth.

There are many days in a human life that, when remembered again and again, can make one groan and weep. I am no exception. Even so, the day I was born, the day of my marriage, the day I first met the deity of my affection—my beloved leader—and the day I first went to prison in the struggle to protect my language: all of them bring me joy. They are memories in which I rejoice.

I have no faith in astrologers who calculate good and evil from the star under which a person is born. Yet the year in which I was born—that year was one of those years that seemed to foretell, with remarkable precision, the good and the evil that awaited the world.

The pages that follow may weigh the good and harm that came to the country because I was born. They may assess the value of the service I have rendered to my motherland. But when I later read and recalled the events in India and the course of world politics in the year of my birth, what I felt was joy.
It was a time when historians had begun to see, with some clarity, what the twentieth century might become.

It was a time when the First World War—having produced destruction and stagnation on a scale the world had never known—had left all the great powers exhausted and drained. At that very moment, nearly all those powers were tightening their grip upon their colonial peoples, imposing harsh measures and intolerable laws, testing how much they would endure.

It was a time when the colonial peoples who survived the World War, having seen human beings die before their eyes like flies and ants, found the courage to say, “Life is no jaggery to us!” and rose to confront the fanatics of imperialism.
It was a time when the vast distance between the old and the new had sharply narrowed and the two stood face to face, clashing in every field.
It was a time when workers were casting off servitude and drawing up the rights they meant to win.
It was a time when feudal landlordism and the zamindari system were breathing their last.

It was a time when, in southern India, it was almost as though the foundation stone were being laid for social justice and social revolution; while in the North, the foundations were being laid for communal conflicts to grow.

There was unity on one point: India must not remain enslaved to the British. But over the means by which that slavery was to be ended, powerful disagreements and knots that seemed impossible to untangle had arisen.
Longing for somebody—anybody—to say clearly that something must happen had become part of the people's daily life.

In 1924, the genius who would dispel a thousand years of darkness from Tamil Nadu and, at a stroke, overturn every sphere of life to meet the demands of the new age—my teacher, Arignar Anna—was then a fifteen-year-old high-school student, shaping himself to become the hero of a great history.
India was shaking off a long sleep and rising with a thrill.

Gandhiji's arrival and his involvement in politics were creating a new kind of awakening. Congress leaders were divided and bewildered over the question: “Complete independence? Or self-government subject to imperial control?”

It was a time when Lajpat Rai, Subhas Chandra Bose, Sathyamurthy, Srinivasa Iyengar, C. R. Das, Motilal Nehru and others would from time to time differ with Gandhiji and engage him in ceaseless argument and counter-argument.

The distinction of Gandhiji formally assuming the presidency of the Indian National Congress belongs to 1924 alone. Neither before nor afterwards did he serve as its formal president. The plans drawn up at the Belgaum session in 1924 were the plans through which the Congress later attained its fuller organisational form.
It was a programme born in 1924 that transformed E. V. Ramasamy—whom the country today honours as Thanthai Periyar—into the Hero of Vaikom.

It was in this period that Thamizh Thendral Thiru. V. Kalyanasundara Mudaliar became a tempest against imperialism. It was in these days too that the labour movement began putting down roots in Tamil Nadu.

Gandhi's teachings of non-violence sank deep in this year. In that same year, brutal violence of the kind seen at Chauri Chaura also ran rampant. Hindu–Muslim division, too, began to gain a foothold in northern India.
No other year of the twentieth century stood like so great a question mark as 1924.
Perhaps because I was born in that year, I too have remained a question mark to many throughout my life!
Gandhiji had been sentenced to six years in prison. But after serving only two, he was released in February 1924 by Viceroy Lord Reading because of failing health.
He came out of prison an altogether new man, having learned the strategies by which Indian politics might be steered with great dexterity along a course between spiritualism and revolution.

During those two years in prison, it is said, Gandhiji memorised the Gita, read the Qur'an, and tried to learn Tamil. Above all, he is said to have thought through and understood that the spark of India's liberation could be found only in her villages.
That was also the year when the young Jawaharlal Nehru, at the age of thirty-five and against his own wishes, was elected for the first time as General Secretary of the Indian National Congress.

How proudly, then, can I say that I was born in 1924—in an atmosphere where non-violence, truth, labour, imprisonment, freedom and the abolition of untouchability were being chanted like mantras from house to house, from person to person!
And that is not all!
The reforms of Kemal Pasha, which in later years I would invoke again and again with delight at every stage of my political life, took shape and began to operate in 1924.
It was in that year that the revolutionary hero Lenin died.
One epoch in world history ended; another was born.

It was also the period when the Trotskyist doctrine of simultaneous bloody revolution throughout the world was beaten back, and the communist movement came down to the principle that revolution must take shape according to the particular conditions of each country.
It was the time when Stalin—whose fervour for his leader Lenin matched the almost-mad devotion I bear my leader Anna—rose to power!

Trotskyism, over-intellectualism, and a statecraft that lacked confidence in itself were all struck down in that year. As though history were declaring that the marks of firm leadership are the power of labour, unwavering loyalty to one's leader, and selfless zeal in serving the people, Stalin in that very year assumed leadership of a movement that held sway over one-third of the world.

In 1924, inside the fortress prison of Bavaria, Adolf Hitler was writing his autobiography, Mein Kampf. The world knows how completely that autobiography would later turn upside down the old histories of so many countries and societies.

Nazism, fascism and communism were all rising strongly in 1924. Yet in India, through Gandhiji, the masses displayed the special respect society can show an individual out of love, and the immense affection a multitude can openly express.

One may say that another idea too was beginning to sprout in that period: if Indian politics was to be conducted democratically, leaders of distinctive stature would have to emerge in the different states, just as Gandhiji had emerged for India as a whole.
It was through this mingling of conflicting currents that 1924 made its way.
And it was in that year that I was born.

The year 1924, in which I was born, was also the year in which the Cauvery water agreement was concluded between Mysore and our state. The agreement was made for fifty years. It is to be reconsidered in 1974.
Tamils are concerned that the decisions taken in that reconsideration should not injure Tamil Nadu's rights.

In the meantime, the Chief Minister of Mysore has ventured to proceed with the Hemavathi project despite the opposition of the Tamil Nadu Government. The Tamil Nadu Government has conveyed its emphatic opposition to the Union Government.

When I was born in 1924, the year of the Mysore–Tamil Nadu agreement, who could have imagined that I would one day become Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu and stand against the Hemavathi dam project because it threatened to impair that agreement?
Even those who gave birth to me might fondly have called me Raja—king. Would they ever have called me Manthiri—minister?
Before I write about myself, should I not give at least a brief account of my parents?
Thirukkolili is one of the beautiful little villages of Thanjavur district. It is also called Thirukkuvalai. The village lies fifteen miles from Thiruvarur.
That is where our family lived.
A lovely temple tank. Groves around the tank! Opposite it, a Siva temple! At the western boundary, the shrine of Muniyan! At the southern boundary, the Ayyanar temple.
That was the Thirukkuvalai I knew.
Today, three-fourths of that beauty has vanished.
But in my father's time, it was a village of incomparable charm.
